brief: Literary theorist Paul Fry's "rules of relevance" idea, that minds preselect which facts register before interpretation occurs, frames Carlyle's read of the AI capex boom. A scaling engineer sees compute buildout as a rational response to a binding technical constraint; a statistician sees an accelerating series with no historical precedent, implying an exponentially widening range of outcomes. Asset prices currently reflect the engineer's framework: required returns and credit spreads have not risen despite the uncertainty. That framework grows harder to sustain because over 80% of AI capex through 2030 must be externally financed, and the $2.5 trillion of disclosed hyperscaler compute backlog nets to only about $375 billion (15%) of economic value once financing obligations are subtracted. The note argues this externalization, not AI borrowing itself, is resetting rate expectations: the US corporate savings glut has reversed (net corporate savings down 86% versus the same point last cycle) as hyperscalers turn from liquidity providers into liquidity users, pushing forward rates higher. Separately, globalization's unwind removes a hidden dollar-demand subsidy that had cheapened US borrowing, and Europe's "peace dividend" is reframed as illusory: its shrinking defense-industrial base tracks declining technological relevance, not freed fiscal space.
